Observational learning is a result of witnessing another person doing something. The learning is performed later and cannot be explained as having been taught in any other way. This type of learning also encompasses the concept of behaviour avoidance as a result of seeing another person behave in a certain way and receive a negative consequence. The four processes of observational learning are: Process 1: Attention •Before students can imitate a model’s behaviour, they must pay attention to what the model is doing or saying. Process 2: Retention •To produce a model’s action, students must be able to store the model’s action in their memory for future retrieval. Students’ retention will be improved when a teacher gives vivid, logical, and clear demonstrations. Process 4: Production •To attending and remembering, students must be physically capable of reproducing the model’s action. Here, the students need a lot of practice, feedback, and coaching before they can reproduce the model’s action. Process 4: Motivation •The students must be motivated to demonstrate the model’s action. Reinforcement can be used to encourage observational learning. This may also be indirect where a student may see other students being reinforced for a particular behaviour and then increase their own production of that behaviour. Or Reciprocal Determinism The world and an individual’s behaviour cause each other. Behaviourism essentially states that it is the environment causing a specific behaviour. According to Bandura (1977) though, this is too simplistic. Behaviour causes environment as well as environment causes behaviour. Just because you taught it doesn’t mean they learned it Misconceptions A misconception is an idea or view inconsistent with the scientific understanding because it is based on faulty thinking or understanding. Alternative conceptions Non-scientific concepts Preconceived notions Preconceptions Erroneous beliefs Intuitive ideas Experience is NOT always the best teacher. Misconceptions are tenacious—when they make sense to students, they’re VERY hard to change. • misconceptions students’ ideas being inconsistent with the scientific understanding. • Students’ misconceptions: 1. are strongly held 2. differ from experts’ notions 3. have a strong influence in students’ understanding Key characteristics of Misconceptions Types of Misconceptions • Misconceptions are ‘popular’ conceptions rooted in everyday observations (Preconceived notions). • Misconceptions include views learned by students from sources other than scientific education, such as religious or mythical teachings (Non-scientific beliefs). • Misconceptions also arise when students are taught scientific information in a way that does not help them to deal with their own preconceived notions and non-scientific beliefs or when they overgeneralise information (Conceptual misunderstandings). • Misconceptions arise from the use of words that mean one thing in everyday life and another in a scientific context (Vernacular misconceptions). • Misconceptions can be falsities often learned at an early age and retained unchallenged into adulthood (Factual misconceptions). NO Air Resistance • An object will accelerate if the forces acting upon it are unbalanced. • The acceleration of an object is directly related to the net force and inversely related to its mass. • Applied to the elephant-mouse scenario, the box with the elephant experiences a much greater force (which tends to produce larger acceleration). • Yet, the mass of an object resists acceleration. • Thus, the greater mass of the elephant (which tends to produce smaller acceleration) offsets the influence of the greater force. It is the force/mass ratio which determines the acceleration. Air resistance • The amount of acceleration is directly proportional to the amount of net force (unbalanced forces) acting upon it. Falling objects initially gain speed because there is no force big enough to balance the downward force of gravity. • Yet as an object gains speed, it encounters an increasing amount of upward air resistance force. In fact, objects will continue to accelerate (gain speed) until the air resistance force increases to a large enough value to balance the downward force of gravity. • Since the box with the elephant has more mass, it weighs more and experiences a greater downward force of gravity. The box with elephant will have to accelerate (gain speed) for a longer period of time before there is sufficient upward air resistance to balance the large downward force of gravity. Terminal velocity: The terminal velocity is the final and highest velocity attainable occurring when the sum of the drag force (Fd) and the buoyancy is equal to the downward force of gravity (FG) acting on an object falling in a fluid. The box with elephant falls faster than the feather because it never reaches a terminal velocity. It continues accelerating accumulating more and more air resistance, approaching a terminal velocity without actually reaching it. The box with the ant reaches a terminal velocity in an early stage of its fall as there is not much air resistance required to cease its acceleration. Once that terminal velocity reached, the remainder of this box fall will occur with that small terminal velocity. Students come in science and mathematics classrooms with a diverse set of ideas concerning natural objects, events and phenomena. Each subfield within the different disciplines seems to have its set of ideas. 2. These set of ideas students bring in the classroom cut across age, gender, ability and sociocultural boundaries. 3. These ideas are tenacious and show resistant to change by traditional teaching strategies. 4. The ideas that students hold often parallel explanations and theories offered by previous generations of scientists and philosophers. 5. The ideas students bring in classroom have their roots in a diverse set of personal experiences including direct observations and their interpretations, peer culture-language and teachers’ instruction. 6. Teachers often hold the same ideas as their students. 7. These ideas students bring in classroom interact with knowledge presented in formal instruction resulting in a diverse variety of unintended learning outcomes. 8. There has been a variety of instruction approaches suggested as classroom tools that can facilitate conceptual change. How to help students get over their Misconceptions 1. Assessing misconceptions When presenting new information to students, it is helpful to assess any misconception they may hold on the material. For example, when teaching students about climate change: • Understandings of the distinction between weather and climate. • Knowledge about the concept of "deep time.“ How to do the assessment • Pollev.com/nikolaosfoto472 https://beta.polleverywhere.com/multiple_choice_polls/oNsyYnmkY4npiPbWPkUcF How to do the assessment The initial acceleration of the person who jumped into the tunnel would be the acceleration of gravity on the surface of the Earth. This becomes progressively smaller as the person approaches the centre of the Earth. Choose a topic of interest and design a diagnostic assessment for any misconceptions student may hold as per this topic. 2. Building on misconceptions Misconceptions are not only a barrier to learning, when used properly they could serve a productive purpose in the classroom. It is important to consider which components of their already acquired knowledge could be beneficial in building a more robust understanding of new, scientific concepts. Misconceptions are not bad! They can be a good thing when teachers PURPOSEFULLY use them to bridge students’ ideas with conceptual understanding of science. Conceptual Change Posner, G. J., Strike, K. A., Hewson, P. W., & Gertzog, W. A. (1982). In presenting new concepts or theories: 1. Intelligible. Teachers should do what they can to increase the intelligibility of the new theory. Students must be able to grasp how the new conception works. To increase intelligibility, teachers can use methods such as: Analogies Models (both pictorial conceptual and physical) Direct exposition (Discovery Learning) 2. Plausible. Students must see how the new conception (theory) is consistent with other knowledge and a good explanation of the data. 3. Fruitful. Students must be able to extend the new conception to new areas of inquiry. Illustrate the application of the new concept/theory to a range of problems. These problems can include familiar ones and new ones. Strategies/Teaching approaches to promote Conceptual Change Bridging Analogies One of the best ways that teachers can correct misconceptions is by a strategy called "using bridging analogies." Intermediate similar or analogous examples Anchoring Conceptions Students' correct beliefs The new concept ) Misconception: Static objects are rigid barriers that cannot exert forces Anchoring Conception: A spring pushes up on one's hand when the hand is pushing down on the spring 1. Anchor example: hand on spring. 2. Bridging example 1: book (and hand) on a spring. 3. Bridging example 2: books on a flexible board. 4. Bridging example 3: hand on a flexible board. 5. Target example: book on table The “Washing machine” analogy In the case of “washing machine” analogy the functions f : A → B and g : B → C can be composed by first applying f (washing process in washing machine) to an argument x (dirty clothes) and then applying g (drying process in a dryer) to the result Diverse Instruction Diverse instruction simultaneously challenges at least two erroneous beliefs that underlie a misconception. Conceptual change is more likely if students are presented with a few examples that challenge multiple assumptions, rather than with a larger number of examples that challenge just one assumption. Diverse Instruction: An Example • Children's erroneous beliefs about the earth can be linked to two more general misconceptions: 1. The belief that the earth appears flat to an observer on the ground. 2. Misunderstanding of gravity and misconception on the influence of gravity on objects located on different parts of the earth's surface. The shape Vosniadou & Brewer (1992) When a ship is at the horizon, its lower part is invisible due to Earth's curvature. This was one of the first arguments favouring a round-Earth model. Photos from satellites • Children receiving instruction about two core beliefs are more likely to show an increased rate of acceptance of a spherical earth model at post-test time. Gravity Cognitive Conflict Cognitive conflict or ‘disequilibrium’ arises when students encounter experiences that they are not able to assimilate or that are incompatible with their current conceptions (misconceptions). Ways to generate cognitive conflict in the mind of the student: 1. Present students with anomalous data (data that do not accord with their misconception). This strategy is thought to be a major means of eliciting cognitive conflict and getting students to change or abandon their current erroneous theories and adopt new ones. Example: Many students could not differentiate the terms heat and temperature and they use these terms interchangeably. Anomalous Data 2. Present students with ‘refutational’ texts (texts wherein a misconception is explicitly refuted by presenting contrasting information) and/or present students with text that presents the new theory or concept. Example: A common misconception on mechanics is that moving objects stop on their own (known as force being used up misconception) Despite the fact that many people think that a rolling ball will slow or stop on its own, this will not happen... Moving objects will keep moving at a constant rate unless they are slowed or stopped, or their direction is changed because of an outside force such as friction.
